old: It's a meal born from mashing together the two on either side of it, not from any foreign tongue.
Take the start of one word for the first meal of the day and the end of the word for midday eating — glue them together.
Breakfast plus lunch, first spotted in Britain in 1895.
clues: This meal's name was coined in Britain, and the idea took decades to cross the Atlantic before Americans embraced it.
A late-morning meal, often on weekends, that replaces two meals at once. It is later and more lavish than an ordinary breakfast, with eggs, pastries and perhaps mimosas.
Cafés and hotels advertise a bottomless Sunday buffet of it, and its name is a splice of the two meals it stands in for.
